title: FDE Deployment Manifest
description: A machine-readable description of a client environment and everything deployed into it. Written to be read cold by a human or an agent who was not present for the original engagement.

manifest.description: Metadata about this document, not about the client.

spec_version.description: Version of the deployment-manifest spec this document conforms to. 0.2 adds the stewardship layer: spaces, lineage, and walkthroughs. 0.3 adds the people registry. 0.4 adds field reports: the deployment's feedback channel.

updated.description: Date this manifest was last revised. Not the same as the last_verified date on individual records.

maintainer.description: Who is accountable for this manifest being true today. A person id from people[] (0.3), or an inline contact (legacy).

supersedes.description: Optional path or URL of the manifest revision this one replaces.

client.description: Who the client is and how they operate. Context an outsider cannot infer from the code.

size.description: Rough headcount band. Drives how much process to expect.

business_summary.description: How this company actually makes money, in plain language. Two or three sentences. If you cannot write this, you do not understand the deployment.

timezone.description: IANA timezone of the primary operation, e.g. America/Chicago. Schedules and change windows are meaningless without it.

operating_hours.description: When the business is live, in the client's own terms. Determines when it is safe to break things.

contacts.description: Legacy (pre-0.3): named humans inline. From 0.3, humans live in the top-level people registry and this field is unnecessary. The lint still insists on humans existing somewhere — a manifest with no people in it is a dead document.

communication_norms.description: How this client wants to be reached, how fast they answer, and who must be looped in. Saves the next engineer two weeks of friction.

engagement.description: What was bought and why. The business case, so the next person can tell whether the system is still worth what it costs.

problem_statement.description: The pain that caused them to spend money, stated as the client would state it.

outcomes.description: The measurable results the work was supposed to produce.

baseline.description: Where it stood before the work.

target.description: Where it was supposed to land.

actual.description: Where it actually landed. Leave unset if not yet measured; do not guess.

support_posture.description: What happens when this breaks at 2am. Who is actually on the hook, contractually and in practice.

budget_notes.description: Commercial context that changes engineering decisions: fixed bid, retainer, hours remaining, renewal date.

systems.description: Every system the deployment touches or depends on. Inventory first; nothing else in this document makes sense without it.

entities.description: The business objects that matter and where truth about them lives. This is the client's ontology in miniature: the shared vocabulary that lets a stranger reason about the data without reading every integration.

flows.description: What was actually deployed. May be empty during scoping.

decisions.description: Why the system looks the way it does, including the roads not taken. The single highest-value section: it is the part that cannot be recovered by reading the code.

constraints.description: Rules the next engineer must not discover the hard way. Regulatory, security, contractual, and political.

rule.description: The constraint, stated as an imperative.

consequence.description: What breaks, legally or socially, if it is violated. Constraints without stated consequences get ignored.

source.description: Who imposed it. A named person or document beats 'compliance said so'.

runbook.description: The operational surface. How to observe, change, and repair what is running.

access.description: How a new engineer gets in, and who grants it.

logs.description: Where logs live and how far back they go.

alerting.description: What fires, where it lands, and who acknowledges it.

procedures.description: Named, repeatable operations. Deploy, roll back, replay, rotate credentials, onboard an engineer.

when.description: The trigger condition for running this.

risk.description: What this can damage if it goes wrong.

known_failures.description: Failures already seen in production, with their fixes. Turns a 3am page into a lookup.

symptom.description: What the operator sees, in the words they will see it.

handoff.description: The state of the world at the moment the original engineer stopped. Written for a successor, in the second person.

current_owner.description: Who owns this today. If nobody does, say so explicitly rather than leaving it implied. A person id from people[] (0.3), or an inline contact (legacy).

unfinished.description: Work that was scoped and not completed. Distinct from debt: this was promised.

debt.description: Shortcuts taken knowingly, and what it would take to undo them.

why.description: The pressure that justified it at the time.

risks.description: Things likely to break on their own, without anyone touching them.

trigger_date.description: For time-bombs: contract expiry, cert expiry, API deprecation.

recommended_next.description: What the original engineer would do next if they had another two weeks, in priority order.

blast_radius_notes.description: Coupling that is not obvious from the code. 'If you change X, Y silently stops.'

people.description: The person registry — the single home for every human in this manifest. Added in v0.3. All person-bearing fields (maintainer, system_owner, decision_maker, delegate, current_owner, tenure.person) reference entries here by id, so a staffing change is one edit, not a scavenger hunt across five sections.

spaces.description: Business domains the deployment lives in, each with a named decision maker. Added in v0.2. A space answers the question a successor cannot answer from code: who do you ask before changing this part of the client's world?

walkthroughs.description: Transition assets — recordings, documents, pairing scripts — that move knowledge from a person into a role. Added in v0.2. Referenced from lineage tenures via trained_via, so every handover leaves a trace.

field_reports.description: Observations from the people who operate the deployment: bugs, friction, gaps, and usage notes, each with a status and, once closed, a resolution. Added in v0.4. This is the deployment's feedback channel, recorded where the next engineer will find it. Reports cluster before they escalate; several against one flow is a redesign signal.

glossary.description: Client-specific vocabulary. Almost always omitted, and almost always the reason an outsider misreads the domain.

id.description: Stable kebab-case identifier, unique within its collection. Referenced from elsewhere in the manifest.

tenure.description: One person holding one role for a period. Roles are the stable unit — defined by the flow's pattern and the work itself; people rotate through them. The lineage of a flow or system is its list of tenures.

role.description: The role held, not the job title: steward, queue-operator, approver, drift-adjudicator, administrator. Matches the role names in the flow's pattern where one exists.

person.description: Person id from people[] in 0.3 manifests; a bare name in earlier versions. The lint enforces registry membership whenever a registry exists.

org.description: Client, vendor, or your own firm.

to.description: Unset means the tenure is open — this person holds the role today.

mode.description: built: the original author of the thing. inherited: took over as the standing holder. covering: temporary, with an expected return.

trained_via.description: Walkthrough id used for the handover into this tenure. Its absence on an open inherited tenure is a finding: the knowledge transferred only in conversation, if at all.

exit_note.description: How the tenure ended and what was lost or learned in the transition. The most honest field in the family tree — write it when it happens, not later.

walkthrough.description: A transition asset: the thing that moves a role from one person to the next. A pattern's transition_walkthrough_must_cover list is the outline; this is the client-specific instance.

location.description: Where the asset lives. A pointer — like secrets, walkthrough content is stored elsewhere.

audience_role.description: The role this trains someone into, matching lineage role names.

duration.description: What it costs to receive: '45 minutes', 'one morning shadowing, one reversed'.

last_updated.description: A walkthrough that predates the system it describes trains people wrong with confidence. The validator warns past 180 days.

space.description: A business domain with a named decision maker: the person whose yes is required before changing anything inside it.

purpose.description: What part of the client's world this is, in their terms.

decision_maker.description: One name, not a committee. If two people must both agree, that fact belongs in notes — but one of them still answers the phone first. A person id from people[] (0.3), or an inline contact (legacy).

delegate.description: Who answers when the decision maker is unavailable, and the limit of what they can approve. A person id from people[] (0.3), or an inline contact (legacy).

notes.description: The politics of the space that do not fit in constraints — where the delegate's authority ends, which changes are radioactive.

field_report.description: One observation from the field. The lifecycle is open, acknowledged, then resolved or declined. A declined report with its reasoning recorded is a decision in miniature.

kind.description: bug: it misbehaves. friction: it works but fights the person using it. gap: something it should cover and does not. usage: an observation about how it is actually used. idea: a suggestion worth keeping.

reported_by.description: Person id from people[] where a registry exists, otherwise a name. When the steward files on an operator's behalf, credit the operator; reports from the people doing the work carry the most signal.

channel.description: How it arrived: a queue session, a run summary, a hallway remark. Knowing where feedback surfaces tells you where to listen.

report.description: What was observed, in words close to the reporter's own. Paraphrase flattens the signal.

resolution.description: What was done, or why it will not be. The lint requires this once status is resolved or declined.

person_ref.description: Id of an entry in the people registry.

person.description: A registry entry: one human, described once. Departed people stay in the registry — their tenures still reference them, and history should not dangle. A defunct team can be modeled as a person when its tenures predate individual attribution.

role.description: Their job, and what they are the decision-maker for.

org.description: Client, vendor, or your own firm.

notes.description: How to work with them effectively — response habits, availability windows. Kept professional; this document gets read by the client.

role.description: Their job, and what they are the decision-maker for.

org.description: Client, vendor, or your own firm.

notes.description: How to work with them effectively. Kept professional; this document gets read by the client.

purpose.description: What the business uses it for, not what the vendor says it does.

criticality.description: core: the business stops without it. Determines change-window discipline.

system_owner.description: Who at the client controls this system — the person whose approval you need. A person id from people[] (0.3), or an inline contact (legacy).

access.description: How the deployment authenticates. Never the secret itself: only its mechanism and location.

secret_location.description: The vault path or secret-manager reference where the credential lives. A pointer, never a value.

rotation.description: Rotation cadence and who performs it. 'Unknown' is a valid and useful answer.

lineage.description: The family tree of this system's administration: who has held it, who holds it now, and how each tenure ended. Tool ownership changes hands more often than anyone documents, and each undocumented handover sheds knowledge.

gotchas.description: Hard-won knowledge about this system in this client's configuration. The most expensive field to reconstruct.

last_verified.description: When someone last confirmed this entry is still true. Staleness here is the main way manifests silently start lying.

definition.description: What this object means to the business. Where the client's usage differs from the industry-standard meaning, say so here.

source_of_truth.description: The id of the system that wins when copies disagree. Must reference a declared system.

also_lives_in.description: Other systems holding a copy. Each one is a future reconciliation bug.

identifier.description: The field used to join this entity across systems, and its format. The single most useful line in the section.

sensitivity.description: Drives logging, retention, and where this data is allowed to travel.

volume.description: Rough scale and growth rate. Distinguishes a spreadsheet problem from a database problem.

quirks.description: Real-world data conditions that break naive implementations: duplicates, nulls, historical format changes.

pattern.description: Id of the flow pattern this was instantiated from, if any — see patterns/. A provenance link for humans and agents; not validated across files.

lineage.description: The family tree of this flow: every tenure of a person in a role on it, past and present. An open tenure (no 'to' date) is a current holder. Staffing is fluid; this is where the fluidity becomes visible instead of surprising.

business_purpose.description: The job this does for the client, in their language. If it reads like a technical description, rewrite it.

detail.description: Cron expression, endpoint, watched folder, or who pushes the button.

steps.description: The path through the system at a level a non-author can follow. Not a code walkthrough.

systems.description: System ids this flow touches. Must reference declared systems. Powers impact analysis when a system changes.

entities.description: Entity ids this flow reads or writes.

location.description: Repository and path, or the platform and project name if it lives in a low-code tool.

runtime.description: Where it executes and on what schedule infrastructure.

deploy_procedure.description: Name of the runbook procedure that ships a change to this flow.

human_in_the_loop.description: Points where a person must still act. These are the steps that quietly stop working when that person leaves.

on_failure.description: What the system does: retry, queue, halt, fall back to manual.

who_notices.description: The named person or channel that finds out. 'Nobody' is a finding, and should be recorded as a risk.

tolerable_downtime.description: How long this can be broken before the business feels it.

known_exceptions.description: Cases deliberately not handled, and what happens to them instead. Prevents a successor from 'fixing' an intentional gap.

context.description: The situation and pressures at the time. Written so it still makes sense a year later.

rejected.description: Alternatives considered and why they lost. Without this the decision looks arbitrary and gets reversed by accident.

revisit_when.description: The condition that should reopen this. Decisions with expiry conditions age far better than ones without.
